
# Introduction

On the day of the second round of Ukraine's 2004 presidential election, the opposition campaign of Viktor Yushchenko prepared to support mass protests. The campaign and its supporters erected a stage and the first tents on Independence Square (*Maidan Nezalezhnosti*, or simply the Maidan) before the polls closed on Sunday, November 21. About 30,000 supporters came to the Maidan that night. But by Monday morning, after the pro-regime candidate Viktor Yanukovych was declared the winner amid allegations of extensive manipulation, as many as 300,000 residents of Kyiv had taken to the square. 

The momentum of the protest only grew; by Saturday, half a million or more Ukrainians had joined the protest. Protesters held the square around the clock, despite freezing temperatures and threats of a crackdown, amid chants, songs, speeches, and a massive civil society effort to provide food, warmth, and other logistical support [@wilsonUkrainesOrangeRevolution2006;@OrangeRevolutionMaidan2005]. The protesters' numbers, perseverance, and organization were a seismic shock in Ukrainian politics; on December 3, the Supreme Court annulled the second round of the presidential election and ordered a re-run. Five days later, the parliament endorsed a set of reforms negotiated among the national elites: a date for the new election, new rules to improve electoral integrity, and constitutional reforms to limit the power of the presidency [@wilsonUkrainesOrangeRevolution2006]. Yushchenko won the December 26 re-run, resulting in major losses in patronage resources and access to rents for the outgoing elites.

These events---Ukraine's Orange Revolution---became a foundational case for a generation of research on the risks of election manipulation for incumbents: the possibility that rigged elections may spark mass protest that ultimately ousts the regime. Such events are hard to ignore; they often involve great physical courage and resilience on the part of the protesters, provide compelling images for national and international media, and really do sometimes result in the downfall of authoritarian governments, as the Orange Revolution, the 1986 People Power Revolution in the Philippines, or the 2005 Tulip Revolution in Kyrgyzstan illustrate. 

Such dramatic and consequential events highlight for many observers the considerable risk that incumbents entertain when they manipulate elections. The cost of such manipulation is paid in lost popular legitimacy [@birch2011]; when an election appears sufficiently fraudulent, costly and potentially destabilizing citizen resistance can occur. Or, as others framed it, the use of election manipulation *reveals* the regime's existing lack of popular legitimacy, making opposition parties more confident in their chances of successfully ousting the incumbent through protest [@fearon_self-enforcing_2011;@Little2012;@little2015elections;@magaloni2010]. Qualitative studies further developed the importance of opposition parties and civil society organizations in detecting and publicizing evidence of manipulation, in order to improve the likelihood of protest success [@Bunce2006]. This overall approach, in which electoral manipulation imposes a cost on manipulators in the form of costly risk to their tenure in office, has become a commonplace assumption in the literature on election manipulation.

But, from a different perspective, the Orange Revolution is also a challenging case for models of election manipulation that emphasize protest risk, in ways that have not been previously addressed in the scholarly literature. Such models of electoral manipulation generally predict that incumbents should back off from manipulation when they face a significant protest threat. Instead of revealing their unpopularity and incurring costly protest, they should try to win with lower levels of manipulation or willingly hold clean elections and accept defeat [@fearon_self-enforcing_2011;@Little2012;@Little2015;@magaloni2010]. 

Yet this is precisely the opposite of what happened in Ukraine in 2004. Both the authorities and the opposition knew what the other was up to: "The mass protests watched around the world after the Ukrainian election were obviously pre-planned, but then so was the fraud that led to them," as Wilson writes [-@wilsonUkrainesOrangeRevolution2006, p. 122]. Knowing that the opposition was laying the groundwork for mass protest in a highly polarized environment, we might expect the incumbent to manipulate minimally in order to avoid signalling weakness. But that is not what happened; one of the central cases for influential models of fraud is plausibly off the equilibrium path. How can this be explained? Why did a government that was revealed to be 'weak' manipulate so extensively, given a known, high risk of protest?

In this book, I offer significant challenges to the assumption that electoral manipulation indicates political weakness, and can thus be deterred by protest risk (I call this traditional view the *regime-weakness model of electoral manipulation*). Instead, building on work by Simpser [@simpser2013], Rundlett and Svolik [@rundlett2016deliver], and myself [@Harvey2019;@Harvey2022;@harvey_manipulation_2016], I develop a *regime-strength* model of electoral manipulation in non-democracies, grounded in the principal-agent dynamics between political leaders and election-rigging subordinates. This model of electoral manipulation builds on four points:

- Illegal election manipulation creates real risks for individual, low-level perpetrators*,even in highly authoritarian contexts.

- These risks create substantial principal-agent problems for incumbents who want to manipulate elections.

- Overcoming these principal-agent problems on a large scale requires incumbent control over extensive patronage resources and over the police, prosecutors, and judges that make up the criminal-legal system. As a result, large-scale illicit manipulation helps induce elite loyalty to the incumbent in three ways:

  - *Costly signal of strength*: By convincing large numbers of front-line agents to illegally rig elections, incumbents demonstrate their resource wealth and degree of criminal-legal control. This helps inform elites' belief that the incumbent has the resources and capacities to defeat protesters.
  - *Commitment mechanism*: Illicit manipulation shrinks the winning coalition compared to a clean election [@BuenodeMesquita2005], presenting a favorable distribution of rents for the incumbent elite coalition. Since siding with protesters to overturn the election would likely result in a worse outcome for incumbent elites, it creates incentives to stick with the incumbent.
  - *Coordination mechanism*: Elites' decision to remain loyal is conditioned in part on their belief that other elites will remain loyal. By sending costly signals of strength and creating a take-it-or-leave-it offer of rent distribution, illicit manipulation makes it appear more likely that other elites will remain loyal---creating a self-fulfilling prophesy [@hale_patronal_2014].

- Consequently, incumbents who produce more illicit electoral manipulation are stronger against protest, rather than weaker.


This regime-strength model addresses other cases that are puzzling under the regime-weakness framework, as well. In the 2020 election in Belarus, incumbent president Aleksandr Lukashenko claimed an ostentatiously successful result: 81 percent vote-share with 84 percent turnout. Within days, the regime faced its most significant struggle in Lukashenko's quarter century in power, as hundreds of thousands of protesters took to the streets over a period of months. It is potentially puzzling that the incumbent regime orchestrated election rigging on such a scale, despite clear signs of opposition strength and its own flagging popularity in the pre-election period [@wayBelarusUprisingHow2020]. If election manipulation is cheap talk that is likely to prompt costly protest, why do incumbents frequently produce such facially unbelievable election results? Put more generally: why does election manipulation persist in places where protest risk is high?

In this book, I argue that the answer to these puzzles has been obscured by scholarly emphasis on the legitimacy costs of election manipulation, especially in the form of protest. Rigged elections no doubt incur some legitimacy costs, which may indeed reduce popular compliance with the incumbent. At the same time, however, illicit election manipulation can *offset* these legitimacy costs by demonstrating the incumbent's resources and capacities to elites [@simpser2013;@gehlbach2015electoral]. By inducing elite loyalty during post-election protests, more extensive illicit electoral manipulation makes incumbents more durable, rather than more vulnerable.  

On a theoretical level, my argument builds on Simpser's [-@simpser2013] foundational work by emphasizing an aspect of illicit election manipulation that is often assumed away: that it exposes its front-line practitioners to personal risks. A few small, individual-level stories illustrate this claim. In the first, a precinct election commissioner in Russia is exposed to legal risk for ballot-stuffing, but avoids official punishment (perhaps due to higher-level connections). In the second, several other Russian election commissioners---lacking such protection---face real criminal penalties for illicit election manipulation.

The first of these stories concerns Marina Tarakanova, who served as deputy chair of a precinct election commission in the seaside city of Gelendzhik (Krasnodar Krai) in 2022. Tarakanova was helping to oversee the voting for the regional legislature in her precinct; she was confronted (and filmed) by Ilona Grachevskaya, a candidate for office from the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (KPRF).^[In post-Soviet Russia, the Communist Party is what is known as a 'systemic' opposition party; one that works within the system.] The video shows Grachevskaya accusing Tarakanova of hiding pre-filled ballots. Seated comfortably, Tarakanova refuses to move until Grachevskaya, the opposition candidate, successfully gets the police involved. 

Upon instructions from an officer, Tarakanova stands, revealing the stack of ballots upon which she has been sitting; the officer rifles through the stack, showing that each has been pre-marked in favor of the ruling party United Russia [@AdministrationGelendzhikGet2023]. The video drew widespread publicity, to the extent that the Central Election Commission felt compelled address the issue in a televised session. The Chair of the Commission, Ella Pamfilova, scolded officials, noting that the ambitions of any party, candidate, or official are not worth the risk to the individual contemplating fraud. "It is not worth it, for this pretty young woman Tarakanova to risk her own personal reputation, along with the reputations of the election commission and the whole electoral system," Pamfilova said. Speaking to regional election officials, Pamfilova said "I want you to carefully examine why she did this. What motivated her? [@antonvoloschenkoHeadCECRussia2022]" 

In the case of Marina Tarakanova, the chair of the CEC need not have troubled herself overmuch to find a plausible motive. According to public records, Tarakanova's occupation was 'main specialist' in the department of mobilization work (i.e. the department which manages public resources for civil defense; Krasnodar Krai is a border region). For this work, her declared income in 2021---i.e., before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine---was 2,900,000 rubles: a very handsome sum for a civil servant in a region where the average yearly income was only 590,000 rubles. Her husband declared an additional income of 646,000 rubles [@mariagridinaWhatKnownOfficial2022]. Despite their large joint income, the couple declared renting only a small flat along with ownership of two modest vehicles [@mariagridinaWhatKnownOfficial2022], though it is not unheard of for officials to omit luxury assets from such declarations [@szakonyiCorruptionCoOptationAutocracy2025]. As a public employee, Tarakanova's lucrative position---and possible future opportunities for enrichment in the civil defense sector---may have hinged on delivering satisfactory electoral results for United Russia, which dominates the regional legislature.
 
Whether she was indeed motivated by such patronage concerns will not be known, since---despite appeals to law enforcement by election observers, the KPRF, and even (tepidly) the ruling party [@antonvoloschenkoHeadCECRussia2022]---there has been no public investigation of the case. The chair of the regional election commission asserted that law enforcement was investigating the incident just days later [@antonvoloschenkoHeadCECRussia2022], however, no charges appear to have ever been brought against Tarakanova. Even before the incident, election monitors have for years complained to the courts in Krasnodar Krai that the regional Investigative Committee (i.e. the state organ responsible for criminal investigations) has been quashing complaints of electoral crimes in the region [@CourtGelendzhikTires2021].

Other individuals, operating in different regions and perhaps lacking important connections, have not fared so well in the Russian legal system. Each year in Russia, a small number of election commissioners are convicted of falsification [@torochashnikovaBallotstuffingDoesntGet2021], while many more are convicted of lesser administrative violations of electoral procedure. While real jail time is almost unheard of [@torochashnikovaBallotstuffingDoesntGet2021], those who are convicted regularly receive substantial fines and/or suspended prison sentences.^[This is a status similar to probation; the convicted person must regularly check in with a probationary officer and avoid committing any other infractions during the period of a suspended sentence.] In 2012, former precinct election chair Tatiana Arkhipova was convicted in court of stuffing 150 ballots in favor of United Russia's mayoral candidate into the ballot box, while destroying 150 opposition ballots. For this, and the subsequent forgery of the election protocol, she was fined 100,000 rubles.^[It is perhaps important to note that Arkhipova's case coincided with considerable turnover in the mayor's office; before her conviction, the candidate on whose behalf Arkhipova had tampered with the election was himself convicted of bribery, removed from office, and issued a fine of 18 million rubles. Three new mayors had since served in rapid succession [@HeadMoscowareaElection2012]. To foreshadow the argument to come, such disruption in the local patronage structure may have altered United Russia's willingness or ability to protect some local agents from legal consequences.] In 2023, two teachers from Orenburg were convicted of falsifying votes and fined over 260,000 rubles---about six months' average annual wage for the region.

Even when convicted individuals face light sentences, there are considerable downsides to becoming a convicted criminal in Russia. For instance, Article 351.1 of Russia's Labor Code prohibits those who "have or *have had* a criminal record, *are subject to or have been subject to* criminal prosecution" (emphasis added) for a variety of crimes from working in the field of education broadly; the listed crimes include crimes 'against freedom of the individual', a heading in the Russian criminal code which includes electoral manipulation. Since many of those who are pressured into manipulating elections as precinct election commissioners are teachers [@Forrat2018], exposure to the legal system also exposes these individuals to the possible loss of their career. Indeed, the law requires educational institutions to suspend teachers from work for the duration of legal proceedings [@CriminalsAllowedWork2015], depriving individuals of income for weeks or months. <!-- All this is further complicated by the legal requirement that workers in Russia maintain a formal record of their employment (the trudovaya knizhka, or labor book), which they must present to prospective employers. Records of disciplinary actions may be included in this book, which can complicate an individual's future job prospects. -->

These examples are, of course, peculiarities of the Russian legal system. But they serve to highlight the intertwined complexities that can arise out of a criminal prosecution or conviction [@pagerMarkCriminalRecord2003;@kirkCollateralConsequencesPunishment2018]; these consequences can be expected to arise in authoritarian regimes, where courts often perform their ordinary functions outside of politicized cases [@shenbayhUndueProcess2022;@ginsburg_rule_2008] while serving to uphold regime legitimacy through law and order [@Whiting2017;@cheesmanOpposingRuleLaw2015]. Front-line election actors, who are typically placed fairly low in their patronage network, expose themselves to these kinds of risks and consequences when they participate in ballot stuffing, election fraud, and other forms of illegal electoral manipulation.

Stories like those of the teachers who were fined a quarter of a million rubles largely go unremarked upon, outside of the local press and the websites of determined election monitors. Among scholars of electoral manipulation and authoritarian stability, they have likewise received little attention. I argue throughout this book that this personal risk has significant theoretical implications. In order to produce illicit manipulation on a large scale, incumbents must convince thousands of agents to break the law, often with a non-zero chance of exposure due to the efforts of opposition candidates, journalists, or election observers. Incumbents can do so by offering sufficient patronage rewards to their agents, but must also be able to promise them a degree of legal impunity. It is this personal risk, and incumbents' ability to overcome it, that makes illicit election manipulation a costly signal of regime strength to elites. By conducting illicit election manipulation on a large scale, the incumbent has demonstrated his ability to solve complex, multilayered principal-agent problems through the application of patronage resources and control of the criminal-legal apparatus. Perceiving this, elites are more likely to stick with the incumbent against an electoral protest. 


This regime-strength model of electoral manipulation offers a pessimistic prognosis: the authoritarian incumbents who are best at rigging elections are also likely to be the best at surviving protest movements. The capacities and resources that authoritarian leaders need to engage the machinery of manipulation are some of the same capacities that help to control society more broadly: extensive patronage networks, pliant judiciaries, and cooperative  security services. Moreover, the more incumbents face a credible opposition threat, the *more* incentivized they are to build and deploy those capacities in order to signal strength / offer a favorable distribution of rents to cross-pressure elites. As a result, the regime-strength model makes predictions that at are diametrically opposed to those of the standard model; namely, electoral manipulation is likely to be more severe when protest risk is higher, and (if protests do occur), more extensive manipulation is likely to be associated with authoritarian regime survival.

 
## Existing explanations of electoral manipulation, and their limitations

Election manipulation has long been understood to impose costs on incumbents in the form of lost legitimacy. In an influential early study of historical electoral manipulation in Costa Rica, Lehoucq and Molina [-@lehoucq2002] argue that the shift to more coercive and illegitimate forms of electoral manipulation "scandalized major sectors of the public," contributing to anti-government insurrections in the 1940s. The concept of the 'legitimacy cost' of manipulation (in contrast to its organizational resource cost) was developed at length by Birch [-@birch2011], who argues that "feared	loss	of legitimacy---domestic	and	international---is	the	most	significant	deterrent	to electoral manipulation" (p. 56). Drawing on World Values Survey data, Norris [-@norris_why_2014] finds additional empirical evidence of legitimacy costs along several dimensions. 

As the literature developed, events like the Color Revolutions figured prominently in theories of election manipulation and how it might be restrained. The role of legitimacy loss---and protest risk in particular---in preventing electoral manipulation has become especially influential in the formal modeling tradition. In some models, use of electoral manipulation is itself a signal of low incumbent legitimacy. According to this logic, fearing the potential costs of mass protests, some incumbents may instead opt to hold relatively fair elections. This approach carries a normatively hopeful message: strong opposition movements---those that are well-organized, well-funded, and enjoy broad public support---can effectively discourage incumbents from manipulating elections. As a result, the chances of democratic transition and consolidation increase. I refer to this as the "regime-weakness model" of manipulation.

```{r weakness-models, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Regime-weakness models of electoral manipulation and opposition protest", out.width = '100%'}
knitr::include_graphics("theory_dag_2.png")
```

There are, generally speaking, two versions of the regime-weakness model, illustrated by the two branches in Figure \@ref(fig:weakness-models). In both versions, weaker incumbents are defined by their low popularity and low likelihood of winning a clean election. As their true popularity declines, incumbents have an incentive to produce more electoral manipulation, to overcome their electoral weakness. However, doing so also creates risks. In the first, depicted in the left-hand path in Figure \@ref(fig:weakness-models), awareness of electoral manipulation induces a loss of legitimacy among the public [@birch2011]; in other words, people are upset at violations of procedural justice [@cho_procedural_2016], and especially incensed if they believe the election was 'stolen' [@kuntz_more_2009;@tucker2007]. The focal point of the rigged election allows individuals with diverse grievances to overcome their collective action problems and mobilize against the incumbent [@tucker2007]. The more costly the expected protest, the more an incumbent is disincentivized to rely on extensive electoral manipulation.

In the second approach, depicted on the righthand side of Figure \@ref(fig:weakness-models), incumbent weakness is formally built into models of electoral manipulation. Here, electoral protest is modeled as a strategic decision by a rational opposition actor. The incumbent's likelihood of defeating the protest movement is typically assumed to be equivalent to its popularity: incumbents who can't win a clean election are also unlikely to defeat a protest movement. Election fraud is thus a double-edged sword; it is a tool that allows unpopular incumbents to win elections while also causing opposition actors to revise their beliefs about incumbent strength downward. Manipulation can get the incumbent across the finish line in the election, but at the risk of signaling weakness to the opposition and prompting a costly protest response. This type of model predicts that opposition parties that are more capable of mobilizing protest, as well as institutional and contextual features that expose manipulation efforts, help deter election manipulation [@Little2012;@chernykh2015third;@Luo2020].

As the figure shows, both versions of the regime-weakness model imply that less popular incumbents face some baseline risk of protest due to their unpopularity, but that incumbents increase the risk of mass protest the more they rely on electoral manipulation [@Luo2017;@Little2012;@Schedler2002;@Beaulieu2014a;@little2015elections]. By the same token, they can reduce the risk of protest by holding cleaner elections.^[Readers who are familiar with the directed acyclic graph notation for causal relationships will also note that incumbent popularity is positioned as a confounder of the relationship between election manipulation and protest initiation. Since it is difficult for even incumbents in authoritarian regimes to gauge their true popularity (much less outside analysts), it is difficult to close this 'backdoor path' and assess the validity of this model.]  


The regime-weakness model produces some conceptual puzzles. Why, for instance, do incumbents claim excessive margins of victory (indicating massive falsification), if falsification is a signal of weakness? Under the regime-weakness model, the occurrence of post-election protest is *the* sign that informal negotiations between the incumbent and the opposition have broken down [@Beaulieu2014a]; the incumbent has manipulated 'too much' given the opposition's strength.  If the incumbent can choose how much election fraud to implement, why do we observe protest---what prevents incumbents from 'correctly' targeting the level of election fraud? And, perhaps most puzzling, why is it that most electoral protests fail to oust incumbents [@kalandadze2009electoral]?

Scholars have, of course, advanced answers to these questions. Incumbents may claim unbelievably large margins of victory because that is what the opposition expects; perhaps it is the deviation from this expectation that triggers protest [@Little2012]. Manipulated elections that trigger protest may occur due to incomplete information, as both sides overestimate their chances of success in a post-election conflict [@smyth2020elections]. Likewise, over-optimistic opposition actors may produce the surfeit of unsuccessful protests that we observe.

Alternative answers to these questions are proposed in Simpser's [-@simpser2013] model of electoral manipulation as a costly signal of incumbents' resources and capacities, which in turn influence other actors' expectations of the likelihood the incumbent will remain in office. Incumbents who blatantly or excessively manipulate elections demonstrate they have deep financial and organizational resources, and a willingness to break the law. In turn, elites, political parties, bureaucrats, and ordinary citizens expect the incumbent to remain in office in the future; these expectations lead to cooperative behavior with the incumbent, helping entrench their rule [@simpser2013]. According to this view, manipulation does not (merely) reveal a lack of popularity, but may also highlight other forms of resilience that can offset low public approval. A simplified illustration of Simpser's approach is presented in Figure \@ref(fig:simpserfig).


```{r simpserfig, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Simpser's model of electoral manipulation and opposition protest", out.width = '100%'}
knitr::include_graphics("simpser_fig.png")
```

As Figures \@ref(fig:weakness-models) and \@ref(fig:simpserfig) show, it should in principle be straightforward to distinguish between these two models empirically. In the regime-weakness model, electoral manipulation increases the risk of post-election protest; in the Simpser model, manipulation reduces the likelihood of protest (so long as it is excessive and/or blatant). However, empirical studies have not been able to conclusively settle this debate. Some studies have found that increased manipulation is associated with greater likelihood of protest, as the regime-weakness model would predict, while others have found no effect [@Hyde2014a;@daxecker2012;@Hafner-Burton2016;@Lankina2017;@ananyevDictatorsSignalStrength2022]. A straightforward selection between the competing models of electoral manipulation has eluded the field, as a result.



## Theory in brief



In this book, I propose an alternative conceptualization of how electoral manipulation relates to authoritarian regime resilience and protest, by integrating Simpser's argument with more recent work uncovering the principal-agent relationships inherent in electoral manipulation efforts. I call this the regime-strength model of electoral manipulation, and argue that it best explains the use and consequences of electoral manipulation techniques. The model predicts relationships between illicit electoral manipulation and three distinct outcomes: protest defeat, protest initiation, manipulation tactics.

### Theoretical background

Incumbents in authoritarian regimes face the risk of revolutionary uprising as well as the risk of insider defection [@svolik_politics_2012]. These risks can be intertwined [@satoEliteCoordinationPopular2019], as mass protest can spark elite defections [@rioStrategicUncertaintyElite2022], and elites who split from the ruling coalition can use their own resources to stoke mass protest [@robertson_protest_2010]. When faced with relatively greater dangers to their position, whether it be mass- or elite-driven, incumbents in authoritarian regimes invest in various means of social control. To reduce the risk of being ousted, leaders will adjust institutions, attempt to purge elites or reduce their influence, shower benefits on cronies, and engage in repressive measures [@BuenodeMesquita2005]. They build parties of power that channel patronage resources and elite ambitions [@Reuter2009;@Reuter2010;@magaloni2008credible;@greene_why_2007], and co-opt their rivals using access to rents [@reuter2015;@gandhi2008political;@blaydes2011]. They censor traditional and social media in order to control the flow of information [@King2013;@Geddes1989;@lankina2020russian]. They fine-tune the independence of courts in order to optimize both political control and perceived legitimacy [@ginsburg_rule_2008]. And they build, deploy, and take pains to coup-proof the security forces to manage threats [@davenportMultiDimensionalThreatPerception1995;@Bhasin2013;@makaraCoupProofingMilitaryDefection2013]. The greater the threats faced by incumbents, the more they are motivated to develop these tools of control in order to retain their position [@svolik_politics_2012], all the more so, since loss of incumbency in an authoritarian regime often comes with steep personal penalties (e.g. loss of assets, imprisonment, exile, or death). 

In their efforts to govern and remain in power, authoritarian leaders must also contend with substantial principal-agent problems. Not even the most powerful dictator can rule alone. They require the cooperation of a vast network of actors, ranging from their immediate subordinates to mid-level bureaucrats and elites, all the way down to ordinary citizens. At every stage, a subordinate's goals may diverge from those of the leader. The leader's closest allies are often the very ones who oust him; the very repressive forces which the dictator relies on to defend the regime from mass uprising may use their resources to topple him [@chinPersonalizationPowerMass2023;@svolik_politics_2012]. 

To keep the repressive apparatus loyal, the dictator must offer them spoils---but not too much, lest they use their resources to overthrow the boss [@draguPreventiveRepressionTwo2019]. Likewise, the incumbent may tolerate some level of corruption among his subordinates, but excessive corruption threatens mass unrest and also deprives the leader himself of some sources of rents; on the other hand, individuals have strong incentives to extract as much as they can from their positions of power. The incumbent may wish for judges to rule in his favor, but those judges may be eyeing the possibility that the opposition will take power, and hedge their bets [@Hilbink2007d;@helmke_courts_2012;@popova2012politicized]. Finally, the individuals charged with manipulating an election on the leader's behalf may have their own incentives to shirk, either to pocket their payments or to avoid exposure [@rundlett2016deliver;@Harvey2019].

Incumbents can mitigate these principal-agent problems through monitoring and punishing defection [@Ginsburg2008], though this can be difficult given the opaque information environment and agents' incentives to misrepresent their behavior [@tutumluParadoxAuthoritarianPower2021;@Boix2013]. Loyalty can be assured through shared characteristics between leader and agent [@svolikPowerSharingLeadership2009], like extended family ties, or shared revolutionary experience [@Levitsky2012]. More generally, incumbents work to ensure that their subordinates incentives are aligned with their own; that is, that they will be genuinely loyal out of self-interest [@Egorov2011]. A fundamental key to maintaining agents' loyalty is the power of expectations [@hale_patronal_2014]. If I expect the incumbent to be in power tomorrow, with the attendant ability to reward and punish, I am more incentivized to work on his behalf today. This, of course, becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy: the more agents are incentivized to work on the incumbent's behalf today, the more likely he is to remain in office tomorrow.

In electoral authoritarian regimes, election manipulation has a central role in this dynamic. One one hand, successful election manipulation is essential for setting up the expectation that the incumbent's time in office will continue indefinitely.  On the other hand, as with other aspects of authoritarian politics, the likelihood of 'successful' manipulation is itself subject to principal-agent problems [@rundlett2016deliver;@Harvey2019]. This means that, as incumbents respond to threats to their power by investing in the repressive apparatus, installing loyalists in key positions, centralizing control over patronage resources, and so on, they also reduce agency loss among election-manipulating agents. When those agents incentives are more closely aligned with the leader's, because of the leader's increasingly well-developed tools of social control, it is more likely that they will carry out their duties. In particular, as developed in more detail in the next chapter, I argue that centralized control over patronage networks and minimizing personal risks to agents (especially through compliant police and courts) reduces agency loss among election manipulating agents.

### Agent risk and signaling strength

```{r mytheory, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="A regime-strength model of electoral manipulation and opposition protest", out.width = '100%'}
knitr::include_graphics("theory_dag_3.png")
```

Figure \@ref(fig:mytheory) summarizes the theory, which is discussed in more detail in the next chapter. Looking to the antecedents of illicit electoral manipulation, we see that increasingly severe principal-agent problems reduce the scale of illicit manipulation. These principal-agent problems are reduced as incumbents can offer stronger inducements (patronage resources) and protection from punishment (legal impunity), but are made worse as agents' risk of exposure increase. Since illicit manipulation requires incumbents to induce agents to overcome their individual interests, such manipulation at a large scale is a costly signal of his resources and capacities; this costly signal has a positive effect on elite loyalty to the incumbent for four reasons. Most directly, it demonstrates the incumbent's resources and ability to overcome multilayered principal-agent problems. Second, it operates a costly 'offer' of the general distribution of resources among pro-regime elites and the broader population. Third, the election result acts as a hand-tying mechanism for the incumbent; new elections may result in worse outcomes for the incumbent and the elites. Finally, these effects in combination create a self-reinforcing mechanism among elites; because individual elites expect *other* elites to cooperate with the incumbent, they are induced to cooperate as well [@hale_patronal_2014].^[Chapter 2 provides more detail on these propositions.] In turn, elite loyalty helps the incumbent to more readily defeat post-election protest. This is how I use the term 'strength' throughout the book: a strong regime has a high probability of surviving non-electoral challenges like protest movements and coup attempts [@leventogluSynthesizingTheoriesAuthoritarian2025].

### Manipulation and protest initiation

The model makes separate predictions for protest initiation. I agree with prior work that some protest entrepreneurs have short-term, strategic motives: they wish to capitalize on signals of incumbent weakness and stage protests that destablize the government. As a result, I expect that more popular incumbents will produce a higher natural vote-share in the election (net of manipulation), which will reduce short-term, strategic incentives to protest.

However, I also argue---in keeping with a long literature on political protest---that there are diverse incentives for post-election protest. Some protest entrepreneurs take to the streets to raise their public profile, to highlight particular issues in bargaining with the regime, or simply for expressive reasons. My model assumes that these diverse motives mean post-election protests may occur for reasons orthogonal to the incumbent's popularity. Hence, post-election protest may occur even against a relatively popular and strong incumbent, but will be more likely as popularity declines.

There are a few important implications of this model to highlight. First, contrary to both the regime-weakness and Simpser approaches, there is no direct effect of illicit electoral manipulation on protest initiation. Instead, I expect protest initiation to be primarily driven by incumbent popularity and by protest entrepreneurs' alternative motivations. To the extent there is an indirect effect of manipulation on protest initiation, I expect it to be *negative*, as protesters motivated by short-term strategic incentives anticipate defeat due to increased elite loyalty. 

Additionally, this model indicates that an apparent positive correlation between electoral manipulation and post-election protest may be spurious. Since the incumbent's natural vote-share also contributes to elite loyalty, unpopular incumbents are incentivized to manipulate more intensively to signal their other sources of power to elites. At the same time, less popular incumbents are more likely to face protest simply because they are unpopular. Consequently, we should see protest more often after more severely manipulated elections than cleaner ones, but this relationship is confounded by the incumbent's (often difficult to observe) unpopularity.

### Agent risk and manipulation tactics

Third, I argue that local agents are sensitive to the risk of exposure and punishment, even if the top patron(s) are likely to remain in office after the election. This has implications for the type of electoral manipulation that incumbents will be able to induce agents to generate. When the risk of exposure and punishment is high, agents will be less willing to carry out the forms of manipulation which are most easily attributable to specific individuals. In particular, in higher-risk contexts (for agents), it will become increasingly difficult for patrons to induce election officials to engage in fraud, falsification, and ballot-stuffing. This is because such activities are easy attributable to the perpetrator: known individuals whose electoral malfeasance occurs at a fixed place and time. When they have the resources to do so, incumbents will compensate for this by recruiting different agents to engage in less attributable forms of manipulation: multiple voting, vote-buying, and voter-pressure. Such techniques are less cost-effective for patrons, and---by directly involving voters---generate legitimacy costs. Nevertheless, incumbents are forced to rely on such techniques when election officials are unwilling to participate in fraud schemes.

Lastly, the claim that agents face criminal-legal risks, and respond to it, is itself testable. By comparing court records with election-forensic analysis of subsequent elections, it is possible to demonstrate that electoral manipulation appears to decrease after a local agent faces harsh punishment in the courts for electoral malfeasance (but *increases* when agents are let off easy).


## Plan of the book

Chapter 2 develops the regime-strength model of manipulation in more detail; subsequent chapters explore empirical implications of the model. Chapter 3 tests the core assumption of the model (that illict manipulation carries risk to front-line agents) using original data from the Russian court system. The results show how electoral crimes are handled in a highly authoritarian context, and how legal penalties for agents in one election reverberate to the next. To construct this original dataset, I scraped the Russian legal database sudact.ru for election-related court outcomes. Of the several thousand such cases, I hand-coded the outcome for perpetrators in the few hundred cases that relate to election falsification. I then match these outcomes to subsequent election results in the region; the statistical analysis shows that when agents face stiff penalties (i.e. large fines or jail time), subsequent election fraud in the region declines significantly. Light penalties, on the other hand, are associated with subsequent increases in fraud.

Subsequent chapters test further of the theory. Chapters 4 uses precinct-level election data from ten Russian national elections from 2001 to 2021. Each election produces data from roughly 100,000 precincts, amounting to a total of approximately one million data points. These results are nested within Russia's regions. This allows for a comparative analysis of election outcomes across regions, while holding the national-level political context constant each election year. I use election forensic techniques to estimate the degree of election fraud and vote-buying / ballot-stuffing in each region-year. Taking these estimates as dependent variables shows that increasing local risk of exposure leads to reduced election falsification, but *increased* ballot-stuffing and vote-buying (so long as patronage resources are abundant). This result supports the principal-agent mechanism of the regime-strength model, showing that incumbents still desire rigged elections when risk of exposure is high, but agents are less willing to put themselves at risk.

Chapter 5 applies similar election-forensic techniques to evaluate the theory in the context of Ukrainian elections, from 2002 to 2014. In comparison with the Russian case, Ukraine allows for a test of the theory in a more competitive, more democratic environment where patronage networks and weak rule of law are nevertheless present. The results are informative, especially in comparison with those in Russia. In Ukraine, where the risk of exposure is higher than in Russia, falsification by election officials is rare. Less attributable forms of illicit electoral manipulation vary with control over the presidency and the regional penetration of oligarchic patronage networks.


Finally, Chapter 6 tests the three main hypotheses of the book on a cross-national dataset of electoral authoritarian regimes from 1989 to 2012. Combining data from NELDA [@hyde_2012_marinov], V-Dem version 15 [@VDemv15], and the Electoral Contention and Violence dataset [@Daxecker2019], the quantitative analysis shows that 1) electoral protest is more likely to occur when elections are highly manipulated but oppositions are strong, but not when elections are highly manipulated and oppositions are weak, 2) that protest movements are defeated more quickly in cases where the incumbent manipulated more extensively, and 3) that incumbents facing a greater risk of protest tend to manipulate *more* than those facing a low risk of protest.



## Broader implications


Multiparty elections are a fundamental component of post-Cold War authoritarian politics [@magaloni2010political;@gandhi2009elections;@donno2013elections]. Elections have been found to have multiple benefits for authoritarian regime survival, including through the co-optation of certain electoral blocs [@gandhi2007;@gandhi2006;@reuter2015], the recruitment of effective politicians and agents [@greene_why_2007;@lust_okar2006], the revelation of information about political actors [@simpser2013;@Miller_2013], and the promotion of domestic and international legitimacy [@isikselVotingAuthoritarianElections2025;@levitsky2010]. Election manipulation is at the core of this process in authoritarian regimes. Authoritarian leaders use of a suite of tools [@schedler2002] to manage the uncertainty inherent in elections, which, after all, provide a focal point for opposition activity [@Knutsen2017]. To reduce the risk of electoral loss at the outset, authoritarian incumbents often deploy pre-election restrictions [@Szakonyi2021;@Bækken2015;@popova2012politicized], repression [@Bhasin2013], favorable institutional frameworks [@golosovAuthoritarianLearningDevelopment2017;@Birch2007;@Ong2018;@Tan2013]. 

However, these tools alone are often insufficient to achieve incumbents' aims. Electoral institutions that were fit for purpose years ago may no longer serve the regime's needs. An unexpectedly popular challenger may emerge. Economic conditions can deteriorate, damaging the incumbent's popularity. Even when pre-election rigging is working as expected, incumbents still need a mechanism to drive high turnout in uncompetitive elections. Finally, incumbents can use their control over resources and ability to break the rules to send signals of dominance that make other actors in society more apt to cooperate [@simpser2013;@gehlbach2015electoral]. To accomplish these goals, incumbents frequently turn to illegal forms of manipulation occur on or just before election day: vote-buying, voter pressure, ballot-stuffing, and outright falsification of results.

Consequently, the findings of this book improve our understanding of more than electoral manipulation alone. By identifying when electoral manipulation efforts are likely to succeed or fail, and what kinds of regimes are most likely to survive, this book sheds light on major theoretical issues in comparative politics. These include, most directly, the stability of authoritarian regimes and the likelihood of further auctocratization. They also provide insights into the role elections play in democratization, and the have some implications for democratic backsliding.


The debate over the nature of electoral manipulation---as an indicator of political strength or weakness---has significant theoretical stakes for major questions of democratization and autocratization. The regime-weakness model of manipulation is optimistic; incumbents who wish to avoid revealing their weakness to strategic protesters may reduce or even eschew manipulation\textemdash an auspicious prediction that under-pins the idea of 'self-enforcing' democracy [@fearon_self-enforcing_2011]. However, if manipulation can indicate regime resilience, incumbents have incentives to both develop and deploy the machinery of manipulation---a gloomy prediction for democratization and democratic resilience. 

On an optimistic note, however, this theory does point toward alternative means of improving electoral integrity, beyond reliance on the public to act as a sort of natural immune system against rigged elections [@fearon_self-enforcing_2011]. To effectively improve electoral integrity, reformers and opposition actors must interrupt the machinery of manipulation by breaking the links between political principals and election-rigging agents. Courts, independent journalists, election observers, and legal mobilization by opposition actors can all play an important role in this regard, by increasing the risk that electoral crimes will be attributed to their perpetrators.
